canberra.title: ‘Cowboy culture’ claim: CIT facing court over student’s severed finger
canberra.snippet: The Canberra Institute of Technology is facing action from the work safety regulator over an incident at Floriade in which a student lost...
canberra.content:
Independent MLA Thomas Emerson says staff report serious safety concerns being ignored and dismissed. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The Canberra Institute of Technology is facing action from the work safety regulator over an incident at Floriade in which a student lost a finger.

CIT board member and chair of the audit and risk committee, Rose Jackson, revealed the incident during questioning by independent MLA Thomas Emerson, who later accused the struggling organisation of having a “cowboy culture”.

“Your question is about one that is with regard to a student whose finger was severed, and that work is continuing, and I’ll have to provide any more information on notice,” she said.

Ms Jackson later confirmed the incident occurred at Floriade.

The incident prompted a WorkSafe ACT investigation.

Ms Jackson confirmed that CIT was involved in a matter related to an enforceable undertaking to WorkSafe ACT, set down for hearing in the ACT Magistrates Court on 23 November.

A CIT spokesperson would only say that the organisation took the safety of students, staff, and visitors seriously.

“CIT won’t comment on individual matters,” the spokesperson said.

Mr Emerson said later that multiple current CIT staff had reached out with concerns about a “cowboy culture” at the Institute and that those who raised the issue faced recrimination.

“People who raise serious safety concerns report being ignored, dismissed and even targeted for having done so,” he said.

“I’ve received complaints from concerned CIT employees about senior officials acting like they’re ‘answerable to nobody’.”

Mr Emerson said that the current statutory and governance arrangements for CIT may have contributed to the situation.

“It’s very possible this culture has been fed by the establishment of an independent board back in 2015 and the related reduction in ministerial accountability and parliamentary scrutiny of what’s going on at CIT,” he said.

“This is something the government’s promised governance review needs to look at closely.”

Officials and Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson also fielded questions on the organisation’s cost-cutting plans, particularly the voluntary redundancy program.

Ms Jackson said a staff meeting was held on Tuesday morning (4 August) to explain the redundancy offer.

She said CIT was now waiting on responses, but the offer had been extended to all staff. There were no plans for forced redundancies.

When asked if this could result in fewer teachers, Ms Jackson said the goal was to “right-size” the organisation after years of declining student numbers.

“We are trying to deliver courses smarter, with regard to online, for example, rather than face-to-face, so all of those are being taken into consideration,” she said.

Applications for redundancy would be assessed based on staff roles and the capabilities they brought to CIT.

No decision has been made on how many voluntary redundancies will be issued, and the process could take up to 12 months, with offers staggered over time.

The offers would be funded through a combination of cash from the CIT budget and requests to the government for assistance.

Ms Jackson confirmed that the entire organisation was being overhauled.

“We’re going through a very large project of re-profiling the organisation, re-establishing what the best organisational structure that will work for CIT is,” she said.

Mr Pettersson said he had been advised of the redundancy program well in advance but was reluctant to say more.

“We’ve observed that this Assembly for many years, even preceding your time in this place, Mr Emerson, has made a range of recommendations about the size and composition of the CIT’s workforce,” he said.

“I see in the actions of the CIT board the responsiveness to those previous recommendations.”

The Sustainable Workforce Program could also include putting new hires and contract renewals on ice with all proposed vacancies, fixed-term contracts, contractor engagements and workshops under review.

canberra.title: ‘Uniquely Canberran’: Iconic bus shelters added to ACT Heritage Register
canberra.snippet: Canberra’s iconic precast concrete bus shelters have been added to the ACT Heritage Register, recognising their architectural, hist...
canberra.content:
4 August 2026

Join the conversation

3

The iconic bus shelters are instantly recognisable features of Canberra’s streetscapes. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Canberra’s iconic precast concrete bus shelters have been added to the ACT Heritage Register, recognising their architectural, historic and social significance to the national capital.

Designed in 1975 by architect Clement (Clem) Cummings, the cream-and-orange shelters are instantly recognisable features of Canberra’s streetscape. There are more than 460 shelters across the city.

They were first installed in Canberra in May 1975 as part of a program to improve Canberra’s public transport system and address vandalism.

Council chair Catherine Skippington said the shelters are a distinctive example of Canberra’s planned urban development and design heritage.

“The bus shelters are uniquely Canberran. They are familiar landmarks in suburbs across the city and reflect the coordinated planning approach that helped shape Canberra as Australia’s planned national capital,” she said.

“Their Brutalist design is seen in their simple materials and modular forms, creating structures that are both practical and distinctive. They demonstrate how good public infrastructure can become part of a city’s identity.”

The ACT Heritage Council found the shelters were significant not only for their design qualities, but also for their strong community value and enduring role in Canberra’s suburban landscape.

Designed to be modular and relocatable, the shelters were intended to move with Canberra as it grew. Many have been relocated over time to serve new and expanding suburbs, a characteristic that remains an important part of their heritage significance.

The shelters were manufactured in Queanbeyan by Melocco. A total of 95 Series I design bus shelters were initially installed around Canberra city in 1975 at a cost of $2,300 per shelter, or a total of $218,500, equivalent to $1.8 million in 2024.

Since their introduction, the shelters have been painted cream, with orange fibreglass window frames and benches, to represent the sunset over the Brindabellas.

Following concerns about the initial cost of the shelters, Clem Cummings made minor amendments to the Series I design, with Series II featuring precast concrete floors, no backrests on bench seating, and no seats in shelters located near schools.

Five different series were produced. At least 170 additional shelters were installed throughout the 1980s and early 1990s.

Heritage registration does not change how the shelters are used, managed or maintained.

The registration recognises the shelters as an important part of Canberra’s modernist heritage and ensures their significance will be considered into the future.

Ms Skippington said the community response to the proposal demonstrated the strong connection Canberrans have with the shelters.

“The council was delighted by the overwhelmingly positive response received during public consultation. Many people described the shelters as ‘iconic’, ‘very Canberra’, and some shared personal anecdotes,” she said.

“We thank everyone who took the time to share their views, stories and memories. The feedback shows these iconic structures are woven into Canberra’s collective sense of place.”

The heritage registration takes effect once published on the ACT Legislation Register.

canberra.title: Next evolution of Ignite Cup builds momentum for Canberra-based NBL team
canberra.snippet: The next step in Canberra’s quest to secure a hometown NBL team has been taken, with the Capital securing the Ignite Cup Finals and...
canberra.content:
NBL great Cal Bruton and Sports Minister Chris Steel announcing Canberra has secured two major basketball events for 2027. Photo: ACT Government.

The next step in Canberra’s quest to secure a hometown NBL team has been taken, with the Capital securing the Ignite Cup Finals and the Andrew Gaze MVP Awards.

The Hungry Jack’s National Basketball League (NBL) has confirmed the AIS Arena will host the tournament and the awards will be presented at Parliament House.

The four-team Ignite Cup Finals series will be held across two massive nights of basketball, with semi-finals on 19 February and a blockbuster decider on 21 February 2027.

NBL Group CEO David Stevenson said the Ignite Cup had quickly become one of the “standout innovations” in the NBL.

“Introducing a Final Four series and bringing it to Canberra is a fantastic evolution of the competition. Fans will experience a festival of basketball, with the best teams battling it out over one incredible weekend for the biggest prize pool in NBL history,” he said.

“Canberra has shown time and again that it embraces elite basketball. The incredible success of last year’s sold-out CODE Sports NBL Blitz proved there’s a huge appetite for the game, and we’re excited to build on that momentum by bringing the Ignite Cup Finals and the Andrew Gaze MVP Awards to the nation’s capital.”

The Ignite Cup features 20 Wednesday night games, with results counting towards the regular-season ladder, as teams compete for a share of $400,000 in prize money.

NBL great Andrew Gaze said Canberra used to be home to the “mecca” of all basketball venues in the country.

He hoped the work underway on planning and detailed design for Canberra’s new National Convention and Entertainment Centre would help make the Territory once again a hub for basketball.

“Some absolute superstars have played here … but let’s not forget about the grassroots, because the grassroots here in Canberra and the talent they’re producing need more courts,” Mr Gaze said.

“There’s a lot of people that want to participate at all different levels, and when that base is strong, the elite becomes even better.”

Alongside the ACT’s $31.1 million commitment to progress planning and detailed design for Canberra’s new National Convention and Entertainment Centre, the 2027 Ignite Cup Finals also provides momentum towards a possible Canberra-based NBL team.

Mr Stevenson said discussions were still afoot about when that would happen, but this was another great step.

“I think we’re building a really strong business case, and it’s not just about what happens at the game; it’s the economic contribution … the amount of people who are coming from interstate,” he said.

“We’ve had an incredible success story out of the Jack Jumpers down in Tasmania – our last expansion team – [they] sold out every single game they’ve ever played, so we’ve got a strong confidence that we can work together … to make sure that, hopefully, once the venue gets approved, that we can build a great team.”

NBL great Andrew Gaze, Chief Minister Andrew Barr and Sports Minister Chris Steel are keen for the events to further grow Canberra’s basketball offerings. Photo: ACT Government.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr agreed that strong economic growth was expected from these two events.

“It is a strategic investment that supports not only our T2030 goal of growing visitor spend by $1 billion by 2030, but also our 2024 election commitment to work with the NBL on bringing elite men’s basketball back to Canberra,” he said.

“Bringing the 2027 Ignite Cup Finals and the Andrew Gaze MVP Awards to our city means the entire NBL family – from players, officials, and fans from every club – will be here for a full weekend.

“The Ignite Cup Finals will fill our hotels, restaurants, cafes and bars, supporting local jobs and giving our accommodation and hospitality sectors a fantastic boost.”

The Andrew Gaze MVP awards will be presented from the Great Hall in Parliament House.

It will bring the entire League together and help promote Canberra’s unique and exclusive event locations.

It’s the first time the Awards have been presented outside of Melbourne in more than a decade.

Sports Minister Chris Steel said bringing both events to Canberra would further enhance the city’s reputation as a destination for major sporting events.

“Events like this inspire the next generation to get involved in the sport and in February Canberrans can watch their sporting heroes compete right here in their own city,” he said.

“Canberrans love their basketball, and it’s great to see the NBL backing that in. What a fantastic outcome for the ACT.”

Fans are encouraged to pre-register for tickets, with the full Finals program to be released during the season.

canberra.title: Woman who allegedly killed tourism leader Jackie McKeown denies dangerous driving
canberra.snippet: A woman has been committed to a higher court for trial over a crash that killed tourism leader Jackie McKeown. NSW Police previously said...
canberra.content:
4 August 2026

Jackie McKeown was killed in a crash in November 2024. Photo: VisitCanberra LinkedIn.

A woman has been committed to a higher court for trial over a crash that killed tourism leader Jackie McKeown.

NSW Police previously said that Ms McKeown was walking along Bicentennial Drive in Jerrabomberra on the morning of 17 November 2024 when a ute hit her.

Paramedics arrived and began CPR, but the 48-year-old died at the scene.

The ute’s alleged driver, the then-54-year-old Teresa Anne McDonald, suffered broken ribs and facial injuries in the crash.

She was taken to hospital for treatment and mandatory testing.

In the aftermath of her death, members of Canberra’s tourism community released tributes to Ms McKeown.

She had worked as the Canberra and Region Visitors Centre’s director of visitor services for the three years before her death.

In May 2025, Ms McDonald was charged with dangerous driving occasioning death and negligent driving occasioning death.

At the time, a NSW Police spokesperson said her licence was also suspended following the alleged offending.

On Monday (4 August), she formally pleaded not guilty to dangerous driving occasioning death, as well as an alternative charge of negligent driving occasioning death.

Ms McDonald is next scheduled to face the NSW District Court on 9 September.

canberra.title: The Lager House has found its groove and already feels like an old favourite
canberra.snippet: Nearly six months after opening its doors, Lager House by Capital Brewing Co has settled comfortably. It seems like the right time to see...
canberra.content:
Lager House by Capital Brewing Co has settled in, and it’s an official winner with Canberrans. Photo: Lager House.

Nearly six months after opening its doors, Lager House by Capital Brewing Co has settled comfortably. It seems like the right time to see how this sleeker interpretation of Capital’s well-established Canberra presence was shaping up.

If turning up on a Tuesday night in the middle of winter and only just managing to snag the last available table is any indication, it’s official: Canberra has fallen hard for its newest neighbourhood pub.

And there’s plenty to love here.

Capital Brewing has traded the industrial, brewpub feel of the Tap Room on Dairy Road for something more polished, but without sacrificing the approachability that made the original a Canberra favourite. The higher-end finishes, moody lighting and lofty ceilings take the experience up a notch, while the atmosphere remains relaxed, friendly and unmistakably local.

Specialty side-pour beer taps were imported from Europe for the perfect pour at Lager House. Photo: Lucy Ridge.

Much like the decor, the beer offering also departs from its predecessor, with one obvious difference being the volume.

Dairy Road has around 20 drinks on tap, including beers, wines, ginger beers and cider. The Lager House has around half of that, but with the focus on their four rotating tank-fresh beers, which not only look sexy with the massive stainless steel tanks living on the pub floor, but also offer a more consistent pour so you always get the perfect beer.

I’m glad to see that, since opening, they’ve added a mid-strength beer to the tap line-up, allowing non-locals to still have a nice time and drive home safely at the end of it. Good Drop is a damn good lager, so it deserves a place on the taps.

Another glaring departure from Dairy Road is that the Brodburger partnership hasn’t carried over to the Lager House; instead, they’ve gone all in on their own woodfired kitchen, and this is what I really wanted to dive into while I sipped on my roasty, toasty, malty dark lager amusingly called All Night Long.

Bringing the food in-house has paid off. The menu is seasonal, delivering on the big bold flavours that you want at a pub while offering variety outside of your usual pub grub offerings.

The barramundi was a little lost under all the parsley but delicious nonetheless. Photo: Martin Conway.

The crispy-skinned barramundi at $34 is flame-roasted, sits atop a bed of romesco and olives, and is topped with almonds. My fish was cooked to perfection, moist and flaky with crispy skin. The use of parsley was a little heavy-handed for my taste, crossing the line from garnish to blanket, burying the whole dish under its foliage, but it was easily pushed aside.

The woodfired chicken skewers at $32 are served like a deconstructed kebab with tabbouleh, tzatziki, hummus, flatbread and chimichurri on the side. Assembling it into little bite-sized parcels to pop in your mouth seemed like the best approach, and it delivered on flavour, reminiscent of your favourite Turkish kebab joint.

The chicken skewers take your favourite kebab and deconstruct it. Photo: Martin Conway.

The surprise hero of the meal was the crispy Brussels sprouts with hot honey and toasted almonds. At $15, this is a generous serve and a wonderful blend of flavours and textures that had us dragging our fingers through the remaining hot honey, only sheepishly withdrawing as the server came to collect our plate.

For those better organised than me, you can go deeper into the woodfired menu by pre-ordering a dish from the woodfired feasts menu, which needs to be arranged at least 24 hours in advance. The feasts are designed for sharing and include rib-eye, lamb shoulder, crispy pork knuckle, miso-glazed pumpkin and charred cabbage.

The overall experience, while a departure from what you already know and love, holds onto the core of what made Capital so good in the first place. It’s like an old friend who has had a glow-up, but is as cool as ever.

Lager House by Capital Brewing Co is located at 62 Constitution Avenue, Campbell, and is open 7 days a week from 11:30 am.

australia.title: Reading and writing worsens in Australian schools as one in three students fail to meet Naplan benchmarks
australia.snippet: Education minister Jason Clare says the results showed ‘real challenges’ but numeracy scores were heartening Follow our Australia news li...
australia.content:
Reading and writing scores are going backwards for almost every age group in Australia’s national standardised school tests, with one in three students still failing to meet Naplan benchmarks.

This year’s tests were taken in March by 1.2 million students across years 3, 5, 7 and 9 to measure literacy and numeracy proficiency, with results released on Wednesday by the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority (Acara).

Participation was down compared with last year due to industrial action in Tasmania and flooding in the Northern Territory, which has led Acara to not report Tasmanian state-level results as it lagged “far below” the body’s data standards for accurate reporting.

The tests were also marred by disruption over a technical issue on the first day for students completing writing papers in years 5, 7 and 9. Acara said national average scores in writing remained similar to last year but it has included a caveat for results, instead of implementing marking adjustments.

One in three students weren’t meeting benchmarks across reading, numeracy and writing, which had not budged since 2025, and one in 10 needed “additional support”, meaning they would need further help to progress and were not working towards expectations.

Average reading scores in years 5, 7 and 9 went backwards compared with 2025, and more students were needing additional support in both reading and writing. Average reading scores were stable for year 3 students.

The average proportion of students “exceeding” and “strong” at reading was 66.3%, down from 68.2% last year

There were some improvements in national numeracy levels since the tests were reset in 2023 for students in years 5, 7 and 9, with the highest national average score of 67% meeting benchmarks and 29,000 more students “exceeding”.

The gains were also evident among Indigenous students, with more “exceeding” in years 7 and 9 compared with 2023 and average scores among year 5 and 7 students at the highest level since the tests were reset.

But for year 3 students, the average national numeracy score was the lowest it had been since 2023.

The education minister, Jason Clare, said the results showed “real challenges” as well as “how to fix them”, pointing to an ongoing numeracy review across primary school levels, spearheaded by Acara as a result of previous Naplan data.

“There is good news here in numeracy,” Clare said. “It’s going up and up in years 5 and in high school.

“Year 3 maths is a different story. That’s why we are fixing the maths curriculum for the first three years of school.

“The reading results show we still have real challenges. They also show us how to fix them … This year’s results show that in schools using explicit teaching methods, including phonics, and small-group tutoring to give kids who are struggling extra intensive help, results are going up and up.”

The federal government’s additional $20bn injection to the public system, to be rolled out over a decade, includes requirements that states and territories implement year 1 phonics and numeracy checks and back “evidence-based” teaching practices, including explicit teaching.

Victoria had the highest average scores across year levels and domains, followed by the ACT and New South Wales, governments which have backed explicit teaching methods. The ACT is also the only jurisdiction to have reached full funding of public schools. The remaining states and territories fell below the Australian average in the majority of year levels and study areas.

The chief executive of Acara, Stephen Gniel, said it was “encouraging” to see continued improvement in national numeracy, especially among the stronger students, but the drop in results among year 3 students was “clearly concerning”.

“Education ministers are addressing this through a range of measures including the rollout of the national year 1 numeracy check,” he said.

“Acara is also playing its part by reviewing the foundation to year 2 mathematics curriculum at the direction of education ministers.”

Gniel said reading and writing needed “our collective attention”, as did continued disparities depending on geography and background.

The average Naplan scores across year levels and domains were substantially higher for students from the highest socio-educational background, which is measured on parental education and occupation.

Similarly, students tended to perform better in urban verses regional areas, with just 23% of students at very remote schools “exceeding” in reading and numeracy compared with 70% of students at major city schools.

“It is … disheartening to see disparities persisting over the years in the attainment of students from our regional and remote areas, Indigenous students and those from a disadvantaged background,” Gniel said. “This needs to be a continuing focus for all in the coming years.”

Gender differences also persisted, with female students outperforming males in literacy and males tending to perform better in numeracy.

australia.title: The ‘extremely effective’ campaigns undermining support for renewables – podcast
australia.snippet: Despite most Australians supporting clean technology, the campaign against wind and solar infrastructure has proven to be effective, stri...
australia.content:
Despite most Australians supporting clean technology, the campaign against wind and solar infrastructure has proven to be effective, striking a chord with many of those living in remote and rural areas. So how do we bring everyone along on the transition to a renewable energy-focused future? And who’s putting up roadblocks?

The Guardian’s environment and climate correspondent Graham Readfearn joins Reged Ahmad to unpack Australia’s relationship with renewables

australia.title: Australian town defends its ‘long-valued and admired’ statue of an enslaved African American child
australia.snippet: Maitland city council condemned an art exhibit challenging the 150-year-old statue, which the artist says ‘does not represent Black skin ...
australia.content:
A 150-year-old statue of an enslaved American child in the middle of a regional Australian town has ignited a furore over race, censorship and what defines art.

Originally designed as a hitching post for horses, the statue later became a Maitland landmark, with images of the boy reproduced on postcards, teaspoons and other memorabilia.

But in 2022, Osvaldo Budet, a Puerto Rican artist began questioning how the statue, known as Maitland’s “little black boy”, ended up there – and why locals thought an ornament widely considered in the US to be a racist caricature was OK.

The statue is a “lawn jockey”, of a style originally manufactured by the American company JW Fiske in the late 19th century.

Those who support it remaining in Maitland claim its history and significance go back to a disputed and uncorroborated legend from the US war of independence.

It supposedly represents a 12-year-old boy, Jocko Graves, who was directed to tend to officers’ horses by George Washington before a battle, and froze to death rather than leave his post.

The Jocko figure was a common form of lawn jockey and advertised as a “darkey” model and the phrase “lawn jockey” itself came to be considered a racial slur.

The Sydney-based wholesale ironmonger WS Friend and Co is believed to have bought and brought the statue to Australia, before placing it in Maitland some time between 1881 and 1891.

In the years since, the statue has changed locations, been stolen and been hit by a truck and broken off at the legs.

The Jim Crow Museum at Ferris University, Michigan, which curates racist historical objects, says there is little evidence to support either the Jocko legend or another claim made about the statues, that they were used to warn escaped slaves of danger.

But a 2024 heritage assessment conducted for Maitland city council said given the lack of consensus on the origins of the statue, the time and historical context in which it was erected should be considered.

“The statue of a Black boy with a small stature, partially clothed, impoverished and waiting for duty, was unlikely to have been purchased to celebrate the bravery of a little boy or represent the bravery of people escaping slavery,” the report said.

“The role of Jocko Graves, standing at attention as a hitching post to secure animals, is also demeaning and is a powerful expression of race and class inequity.”

Proponents of the figure, including Maitland mayor Philip Penfold, say it is a beloved part of the community that has been embraced by children, dressed in sporting colours and photographed by families for generations.

But not all residents agree.

The chief executive of the Mindaribba Aboriginal land council, Tara Dever, always thought the statue was an “ugly and awful thing” when she lived in Maitland during the 80s. It is, she says, a symbol of racism and colonial power on Wonnarua land.

“Whether or not it is American, that is a Black child,” she said.

“It has been called a Black boy for 150 years, which is also what most of the men in my community have been called.

“They should not be seen in the same light as a statue of a child with its head down in a submissive position.”

Condemning the artist

On 11 July, after years of research, Budet’s artwork, Monuments, produced in response to the statue, went on display at the Maitland regional art gallery.

The artwork examines the hitching post’s history in the town and origins as a racist caricature by eliminating its image from souvenirs and recreating it using ink created from Maitland coal, connecting it to the region and the practice of blackface.

“I was imagining how Maitland would look without this image,” Budet says.

“My intention was not to talk about this from a higher moral standing, it was to let locals know the story being told by the local government: that you love these images … And to see from the perspective of people that have been hurt.”

He also consulted the Mindaribba land council to discuss his work prior to the exhibition, which Dever says was “probably the most supported action in truth-telling and reconciliation that has happened in this town for a very long time”.

A few days after the exhibit opened, a majority of council members voted in favour of a resolution expressing a “high level of disappointment” in the decision to exhibit the display and acknowledging the “cultural significance” of the hitching post to many generations of Maitland residents.

The exhibit includes the council-commissioned heritage report.

“While art may be thought-provoking, council considers this approximately 4000-word display to be primarily a political statement rather than an exhibition of art,” the motion read.

The council had previously ordered the report be removed, Budet says, but it has since been reinstalled.

However Penfold then directed gallery staff to erect a sign warning the art “may cause offence” to locals who have “long valued and admired the iconic hitching post statue”.

The sign said the council respected freedom of expression and the artist’s right to present the exhibition “on this occasion”.

“I was just surprised by the audacity of these people,” Budet says.

“This is an African American boy as a slave, displayed on High Street with pride, and painted a pitch black, like it’s tar, that does not represent Black skin with any dignity.

“This statue of this Black slave boy doesn’t have a warning on the street, but my work criticising that image does.

Penfold maintains he “did not seek to remove the exhibition, seek to censor it, seek to remove any element of it, nor silence artistic expression”.

“I simply made it clear that the views expressed in the exhibition are not the views of council nor our community,” he said in a statement.

On April Fools’ Day, councillor Mitchell Griffin shared a post joking that a giant version of the hitching post had been installed at the Maitland regional art gallery, while during Naidoc week the mayor shared a Facebook photo asking users to “thumbs up” to support the statue or “angry face to propose his removal”.

Councillor Amelia Atkinson, who voted against the council motion condemning the artwork, said the sign was “operational overreach”, noting there had been almost no public engagement on the issue.

“This is the first time I’ve seen elected representatives interfere with the content of an exhibition,” she said.

Speaking to Guardian Australia, councillor Don Ferris acknowledged locals have become attached to the statue over the years but urged them to view Budet’s work.

“Put yourself in somebody else’s shoes and think about how that would make you feel if you were from a different culture and had dark skin, to see such a racist connotation on our main street,” he said.

australia.title: ‘Did you send that report?’ The Icac bombshell that came late for Damien Tudehope
australia.snippet: The former Liberal finance minister was questioned by Icac counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer, on Tuesday Get our breaking news email , free ...
australia.content:
The bombshell came in the last five minutes of former finance minister and rightwing powerbroker Damien Tudehope’s examination before the Independent Commission Against Corruption.

At 3.30pm on Tuesday, Tudehope was shown an email which he sent in February 2023, attaching a leaked draft parliamentary report into branch stacking in the Hills area by the Reformers, the shadowy group at the centre of Icac’s Operation Rosny.

It has probably imperilled his parliamentary career.

“Would you regard yourself … as being bound by keeping it confidential?” asked counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer, SC. Tudehope visibly tensed.

“Did you send that report in draft to Mr Greenwood?” she asked, showing him the email. “It appears that I did,” Tudehope replied quietly.

Jeremy Greenwood is one of the group of conservative Catholic men who set up the Reformers, recruiting like-minded conservatives to the Liberal party in order to take over branches from the moderate and centre-right factions.

In 2023, during the parliamentary inquiry, the key Reformers and associates – Christian Ellis, the then premier’s brothers Jean-Claude Perrottet and Charles Perrottet, and Greenwood – had left NSW to avoid being called to the parliamentary inquiry.

Tudehope told Icac he had had a conversation with the premier, Dom Perrottet, who said he knew his brother had gone to Fiji.

Leaking a draft parliamentary report is a serious breach of parliamentary rules and contempt of parliament. It may even constitute corrupt conduct depending on the motivation of the leak.

Tudehope has not been named as a person of interest in Operation Rosny but has stood down as shadow attorney general.

Wednesday’s evidence, however, raised questions of just how tightly Tudehope was tied into the activities of the Reformers and the donations they are alleged to have taken to fund their branch takeover activities.

The day started well enough. A politician for 20 years, Tudehope was happy to talk expansively about his alignment with the Reformers’ causes on conservative social issues.

He’d been happy to be a speaker at events advocating for safe schools and opposing gender fluidity and marriage equality.

But when it came to questions about whether funds flowing into the Reformers were political in nature, the lawyer in Tudehope emerged.

“I don’t necessarily accept the premise that every event where someone signs up to a party as a result of attending the event is necessarily a contribution for the benefit of a party, and I think I identified to you that there are people who may sign up to a party to provide no benefit to a party,” Tudehope said.

“So, to the extent that you identify for the benefit of a party, I think that’s a very moot point about the definition of a benefit to the Liberal party.”

Dwyer wasn’t letting him off the hook so easily. In painstaking detail, she ran him through text messages and WhatsApp groups that she alleged showed knowledge of the secret money trail.

Tudehope’s close friend and former law partner Michael O’Hara, who became a successful hotelier, became a major donor to the Reformers, giving $165,000 to a number of entities after introductions at a function at Tudehope’s home where the News Corp columnist Miranda Devine was the speaker.

Tudehope agreed he might have introduced Ellis to O’Hara, but denied he had encouraged illegal donations.

“If you think that I would expose a friend of mine to that level of scrutiny that he was exposed to, 83 years of age with stage three/four cancer, you think that I would have done that in circumstances where I knew that he would be a prohibited donor for the purposes of the Electoral Funding Act, not on your life!” he said.

Under sustained questioning, Tudehope agreed that using invoices to public relations firms to channel payments was “concealment” as the commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, phrased it.

The other major backer of the Reformers was Catholic Schools NSW and here Tudehope has several connections. He was friends with the CEO, Dallas McInerney, also a powerful key figure in the right, while his son James worked in communications at Catholic Schools NSW.

Icac heard on Wednesday that at a Sunday lunch, James Tudehope told his father he was being pressured to pay an invoice from Ellis. He was “very agitated” because he didn’t think they were getting value for money, Damien Tudehope said.

Tudehope said he recommended his son take it up with McInerney, his boss.

In Dwyer’s opening address we learned that Ellis, who has moved to London and declined to appear, had used his public relations firm, Beckington, to take donations for Reformer work.

Tudehope was also an employer of key Reformers in his ministerial office.

In August 2019, the federal member for Berowra, Julian Leeser, who was unaligned to a faction, went public with his concerns about the branch stacking in the Hills in the Sydney Morning Herald.

Icac heard that Ellis had said publicly at a Reformers event that “Leeser was a lefty and had to go”, drawing the ire of several in the party.

Dwyer tabled an article by Tom Rabe written in 2019 about the factional war and the involvement of two of the Reformers, Ellis and Jean-Claude Perrottet, who were employed in Tudehope’s office. He suggested Liberals were concerned the pair spent most of their time on branch stacking.

By October 2019, Tudehope’s office let Ellis go, concerned about the adverse publicity his activities were drawing. Tudehope said it was the chief of staff who made the call.

By 2020, the heat on the Reformers was increasing.

Tudehope was on Tuesday shown messages from 2020 between members of the Reformers in which they said MPs “were getting scared about ICAC,” and that “Scott and Damien are afraid”.

Tudehope denied knowing what they were about. But by the end of the day, he could have little doubt he now had reasons to fear Icac.

australia.title: Melbourne anti-weapons protest being investigated as terrorist act by ‘far-left extremists’
australia.snippet: Federal police say those who vandalised a defence manufacturer and torched nearby cars could face life imprisonment Get our breaking news...
australia.content:
Anti-weapons protesters who vandalised a defence manufacturer and set nearby vehicles alight could face life imprisonment after police said the incident was being investigated as an act of terrorism by “far-left extremists”.

The Australian federal police, their Victorian counterparts and spy agency Asio are examining whether the incident at Melbourne-based Lovitt Technologies on 5 July 2025 was potentially perpetrated by “far-left extremists, motivated by anarchist and revolutionary ideologies”, a joint statement said.

If convicted, they could face life imprisonment, AFP detective superintendent Anthony Hall warned.

“We clearly have some information about these alleged offenders and are focused on identifying who they are,” he said.

“The AFP, together with our partners, will not tolerate acts of terror motivated by extremist ideologies aiming to cause fear and anguish in our community.

“At any time, we could be knocking on the door of the accused group. We know this is making some in the group anxious – and it should, because we are determined to bring them before the courts.”

Wearing black hoodies, backpacks and gloves, members of the group claimed responsibility for the attack in a video posted online.

Their video advises viewers on how to create an incendiary device, similar to the one suspected of creating a fire that damaged three vehicles at Lovitt Technologies, and voices their opposition to the government.

In a video seen by Guardian Australia, a person who claims to represent the “anonymous cell” responsible outlines support for Palestine and claims Lovitt Technologies was targeted because it supported the global F-35 joint strike fighter program, whose jets are used by the Israeli military.

“This was not an accident nor thoughtless vandalism,” the person, whose voice was digitally altered, said.

“If you continue making weapons components of any kind, there will be consequences.”

Lovitt Technologies supplies parts to the joint strike fighter program, whose global supply chain has been subject to fierce political debate in Australia and a major legal challenge in the UK.

But all companies and their employees had a right to go about their business safely, Victoria police’s Acting Supt Anthony Wheatfill said.

“That anyone would use such violent and dangerous methods to express a political or social viewpoint is unacceptable,” he said.

After the incident, the alleged offenders left using a back fence and rode ebikes south-west along Plenty River.

Community members with knowledge of the offenders or dashcam footage have been urged to come forward.

world.title: Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says
world.snippet: European Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more people The president of the Eu...
world.content:
The president of the European Commission has called for action to strengthen Europe’s borders after tens of thousands of people arrived and quickly left the Spanish territory of Ceuta, triggering a furious row between Madrid and other European countries.

In a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday, Ursula von der Leyen said: “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points, including vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.”

She praised the Spanish socialist leader’s swift handling of the crisis, after the vast majority of migrants left Ceuta and Spanish officials began installing a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier at the border ‌with Morocco. “Order has been restored and the returns system in place worked,” she wrote in the letter.

Spain ⁠estimates that about 69,500 migrants ​have returned to Morocco over the past four days, exceeding initial estimates of 50,000 having arrived in the enclave in north Africa on Thursday. Authorities in Ceuta reported that 88 people died trying to reach the territory, while at least 11 deaths have been recorded in Morocco.

Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish enclave, have the EU’s only land borders with Africa. There are periodic surges in attempted crossings to both cities, although neither permits onward free movement to the EU as they are outside the border-free Schengen zone.

EU interior ministers will hold emergency talks on Tuesday, which von der Leyen said would be a chance to draw lessons from the crossings.

She said the EU should double down on five areas: strengthening cooperation with non-EU countries to prevent migration; stronger external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks; and boosting returns of people with no right to stay.

Italian media reported that Giorgia Meloni’s government wanted to accelerate the opening of offshore migration centres, which Europe’s top human rights expert recently said risked becoming “human rights black holes”.

The EU opened the door to offshore detention centres in June in an unprecedented departure from legal norms as part of a law aiming to increase the deportations of people with no legal right to stay.

Amid heavy criticism of the EU’s divided response to the Ceuta border crossings, von der Leyen stressed that Spain could access EU funds as well as support from the Frontex border agency. So far Madrid has not requested the assistance of Frontex.

The crossings – seized on by far-right politicians across Europe – have exposed deep divisions over migration that have left Spain’s leader isolated.

Over the weekend, Sánchez criticised other governments for failing to support Spain, after Italy and Denmark led calls for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen zone. Sánchez said such an attitude was “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest” and contrary to European and humanitarian law “and the principles of solidarity that bind us together”.

Italy and Denmark organised a letter signed by 20 other EU member states that appeared to blame the crisis on Sánchez’s decision to regularise the status of 500,000 migrants without documents. “We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration,” the 22 leaders wrote, arguing for the need to address “all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularisation of [a] very large number of irregular migrants”.

EU member states favouring a tough approach to migration are expected to raise the issue of “pull factors” on Tuesday. “There is some concern that the regularisation of 1.2 million people can be used to paint a picture that the door is open,” an EU diplomat said, referring to the approximate number of people who applied for regularisation under the 2026 Spanish government programme.

Academic research has found no evidence of a pull effect from regularisation programmes on arrivals of irregular migrants.

Michele LeVoy, the director of Picum, an umbrella group that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants, said regularisation programmes had been criticised by EU governments for the last two decades. “If an EU country offers regularisation possibilities, other member states believe that it may invite secondary movement [onward movement to other EU member states] – that is what EU member states don’t want and that explains most likely the harsh response.”

Amid widespread suspicion that Morocco helped fuel the crisis, von der Leyen described the country as “an important strategic partner”, especially in combating “illegal migration”.

Officials said that before the Ceuta crossings, the European Commission was looking to upgrade the EU’s diplomatic relationship with Morocco to a “strategic and comprehensive partnership”. The EU already has similar wide-ranging agreements with Egypt and Tunisia, which include pledges to stem migration, but which have been heavily criticised by rights groups.

Von der Leyen wrote: “On anything related to Ceuta and Melilla, we could enhance border management early-warning systems and improve our technical and financial support to Morocco.”

Rights groups said people seeking work or fleeing persecution needed routes to move safely. LeVoy said: “On Ceuta, political games are being played over the lives of people on both sides of the border – those who hope for a better life, and those who are made to fear a so-called ‘invasion’. But what happened in and around Ceuta is fundamentally the result of Europe’s inaction on decent work permits and other regular pathways and the dismantling of its asylum systems.”

world.title: How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The Latest
world.snippet: Dozens of people died attempting to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after an estimated 50,000 crossed from Morocco last week. The inci...
world.content:
Dozens of people died attempting to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after an estimated 50,000 crossed from Morocco last week. The incident has led to a political crisis in Spain and criticism from EU countries.

Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s European community affairs correspondent, Ashifa Kassam – watch on YouTube

world.title: Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing
world.snippet: Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity Explainer: why is Ceuta ...
world.content:
A growing chorus of voices has accused Morocco of helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”.

Spanish officials ⁠said on Monday that an estimated 69,500 people who had arrived late last week in Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa, had returned to Morocco in recent days. About 2,500 people who had made the crossing were believed to still be in Ceuta.

The extraordinary influx had overwhelmed the city of 84,000 people and set off a political crisis across the EU as some member states laid blame on Spain.

In Ceuta, leaders pointed to the broader picture of what had transpired. “It’s an atrocity,” said Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of the territory. “There are 88 bodies in the morgue, and there are more on the other side of the border.”

He said local people watched the events play out with a mix of sadness, worry and anguish. “People see this not as a migration crisis; it was fundamentally an attack, a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” Vivas told El País newspaper. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco.”

He drew a parallel with May 2021, when Rabat loosened border controls, allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days, during a diplomatic standoff over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.

This time around, analysts have suggested that Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s arch-enemy Algeria could have triggered a response from Morocco.

Speaking on Monday, Spain’s defence minister, Margarita Robles, also seemingly signalled Rabat’s involvement. “Neither Spain nor Morocco can look the other way when it comes to this tragedy,” she told reporters. “I ask the Moroccan government to fully investigate what happened.”

The insinuation appeared to be backed by the preliminary assessment of Spanish intelligence services, who cited suspicions that the influx had not been planned by Moroccan authorities but concluded that Morocco had failed to stem the tide of people rushing towards the border and in some cases had even facilitated their passage.

Intelligence sources told El País that the roots of the influx probably lay in a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported. As the hoax gained steam online, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum until it was completely lifted late last week, allowing tens of thousands of people to stream through.

In Ceuta on Monday, hundreds of people continued to sleep rough on the beach or near Ceuta’s mosques. One local official told reporters that those who remained in the city included 862 unaccompanied minors.

Ashraf, 28, said he had defied his mother’s warnings against crossing into Spain after spotting posts on social media that said the border had been opened. While he had made it to Ceuta, what had followed was a days-long ordeal as he scrambled to find food and shelter while fending off the memories of what he had lived through.

“You might see me smile a little but inside I’m shattered,” the Moroccan national said as he recalled swimming past bodies to reach Ceuta. “There were so many people in the sea. Everyone was trying to grab on to you to save themselves, and you were trying to escape and move forward so they wouldn’t drag you down or drown you. The Moroccan police were pushing us toward the water and telling us ‘swim, swim’.”

Others were desperately seeking loved ones who were missing. One mother said she had been roaming the streets of Ceuta for days, frantically searching for any sign of her children, aged 13 and 16.

She had left Morocco alone, finding out later that her two children had followed her by plunging into the sea to make their way around the border.

“I need help,” she said as she held up a photo of a smiling young boy flashing a thumbs-up sign. “Some migrants told me they had seen them in Ceuta, but I can’t find them.”

Across the EU, the crisis in Ceuta had seemingly ushered in a moment of reckoning after a handful of EU countries responded to the crisis by calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Italy said it had suspended passport-free Schengen travel arrangements with Spain for one month, despite the fact that Ceuta is not part of Schengen.

Before an emergency video meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday to address the crisis, Spain’s foreign minister said the country would demand solidarity from EU members after several had, in his view, “fallen short” of what was expected.

“There was a synchronised reactionary international effort that very quickly amplified what was happening, spreading lies and fake news about the integrity of the Schengen area and about Spain’s actions,” José Manuel Albares told the broadcaster TVE. “Unfortunately, these falsehoods have even been amplified by some European governments.”

What had transpired in Ceuta was “very unusual”, he said. “Spain currently has the lowest number of irregular entries on the Mediterranean route,” he added, while Italy “was the country with the highest number of irregular entries in Europe”.

He said he had been in contact with Moroccan authorities throughout the crisis. “They showed a willingness from the very beginning to mobilise police forces to help stem the flow of migrants.”

Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said in a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, that the Tuesday meeting would be a chance to draw lessons from what happened in Ceuta, and she commended Madrid for its swift handling of the crisis. “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points,” she said.

At a meeting of member states on Saturday, the Guardian was told that while Italy and Denmark, with some support from Poland and Sweden, had criticised Spain for what had happened, there was a strong suspicion that the crisis was not an accident but had been coordinated.

There was widespread recognition that Spain could not simply pin the blame on Morocco, given the close cooperation needed to return those who had crossed and, in the longer term, for migration control and security, a source said.

EU states also spoke about the threat of Russian disinformation and how it could exploit the crisis to heighten tensions across the bloc, the source added.

The concerns came into public view late last week when Ukraine’s acting foreign minister said more than 1,500 publications regarding Ceuta had been identified in pro-Russian networks.

“We have detected an intensive Russian propaganda campaign across Europe using pictures from Ceuta to sow destabilisation,” Andrii Sybiha wrote on social media. “This is not about the situation itself but about the way Russia tries to exploit any topic that can benefit its agenda.”

world.title: Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streets
world.snippet: People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects Four days ago, Youssef E...
world.content:
Four days ago, Youssef El Abbas saw an opportunity to reclaim the life he had lost seven years earlier. News was circulating that about 400 people had swum from Morocco to the neighbouring Spanish enclave of Ceuta on the north African coast, approximately 12 miles (19km) across the strait of Gibraltar from mainland Spain.

Here was a chance for the 44-year-old Moroccan father of four to return to Spain, from which he had been deported when his residency expired after the loss of his job in Bilbao in 2019.

El Abbas took a taxi and headed to the city of Tétouan, south of the enclave. While en route, he saw Facebook posts and news reports claiming that the Moroccan authorities were allowing people to pass through their side of the border. That meant that unlike those who had crossed the previous night, he could simply travel overland before swimming for just five minutes across the border from Moroccan to Spanish territory to avoid the Spanish border controls.

He reached Tétouan to find the city completely overwhelmed. “Young men were running through the streets, flooding every corner,” he said. By the time a second taxi took El Abbas to Fnideq, the town bordering Ceuta, he realised that the usual blockades and checkpoints preventing people without European documents from even approaching the frontier had been removed.

“The Moroccan police were shouting at us: ‘Go, go, go! Run now, run into Spain,’” he said. “The night before, they were beating people. But that morning they were letting us through. Nothing made sense.”

Despite the crowds, El Abbas noticed the police were only letting Moroccans cross over. “All the sub-Saharan migrants were being pushed back by force.”

He reached the border at 2.45pm on Wednesday. By 3pm, after a short swim, he was standing on Spanish soil. Not everyone was so lucky.

“In just 10 minutes in the water, I saw four people floating dead in Moroccan waters,” he said. “People were pulling their bodies out.” They were among at least 72 people who drowned or were crushed trying to reach the Spanish territory.

El Abbas is just one of the 50,000 or so people to have crossed into Ceuta this week, in what Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, described as “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”.

Madrid has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla – the other Spanish enclave on the north African coast – could not be summarily returned under special rules.

But there has also been speculation that the Moroccan authorities may have opened the border to signal their displeasure at Sánchez’s recent visit to Algeria, which supports efforts to free the disputed territory of Western Sahara from Moroccan occupation.

Morocco’s ambassador to Spain, Karima Benyaich Millán, said Rabat was not happy about the mass crossing, adding that it hoped those in Ceuta would return.

Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations” and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.

In May 2021, Rabat loosened border controls – allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days – during a diplomatic standoff triggered after Madrid allowed a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.

El Abbas said he had never stopped dreaming of returning to Spain, where he had worked mainly in the hospitality sector for 14 years. Since being deported to Morocco in 2019, he has lived apart from his wife and four daughters, who remain in the northern Spanish city of Bilbao, while scraping by with occasional work repairing mobile phones alongside his father.

“I never stopped thinking about coming back,” he said. “In Morocco, I was alive, but I wasn’t really living.”

The return has been bittersweet. When he swam ashore in Ceuta, a Spanish Guardia Civil officer extended a hand to pull him from the sea. But that gesture of aid eventually gave way to one of violence. Three days after arriving, the group of people he was with were surrounded by a military patrol and beaten.

“The same hand that helped me out of the water was the one that later hit me,” he said.

El Abbas’s story is hardly unique. Although more than 48,000 people had crossed back into Morocco by Friday night, hundreds are still sleeping in parks, public squares and on pavements, waiting for a chance to move on or simply to find somewhere to rest. It appears to be virtually impossible for migrants to leave Ceuta for mainland Spain.

Said, 17, from Casablanca, was sitting on a kerb a few hundred metres away. He, too, had joined the Ceuta-bound crowds when he heard that the border was open. But the jubilation had given way to reality and all he had was a bottle of water and the carton of yoghurt a local resident had given him.

The teenager said he was taken to a centre for unaccompanied minors after he crossed, but there were no places available, so he ended up back on the streets. According to a soldier who asked to remain anonymous, the current protocol for the authorities – including the military, the police and the Guardia Civil – is to treat unaccompanied minors as regular migrants and return them to Morocco.

Said and the other teenagers with him said no one would sell them food or allow them into shops and restaurants because they did not speak Spanish.

Three days after the mass influx, Ceuta is slowly trying to recover a sense of normality. By early evening on Saturday, cafe terraces were beginning to fill again and some businesses had reopened their doors. Many of the remaining arrivals are being tended to by Ceuta locals, who walk the streets handing out bottles of water, sandwiches, blankets and clothes. Others stop to ask if they need help or to offer to call a relative.

Such shows of solidarity have been threatened by the arrival of far-right politicians and a neo-Nazi group, all keen to use the humanitarian crisis for their own ends.

“They’re going to exploit our feelings to claim the credit and say they defended Ceuta,” said a local woman called Malika. “We don’t want them here. If they want to defend something, they should go somewhere else.”

Malika, who was born in Ceuta to a soldier who served in the Spanish army, rejected the notion that the city should be defined solely by the political confrontation that followed this week’s mass arrival. But she also acknowledged the pressure on a city of just over 80,000 people. “It would have been an impossible situation for any city,” she said.

Fatima Hamed Hossain, a member of Ceuta’s assembly, fears that the strain created by the crisis has deepened divisions within the city. “Everything we’ve lived through has created tensions between neighbours,” she said. “That’s exactly what feeds the far right.”

As a caravan of people returned back over the border, Said’s mind was on the future. His goal is simple: get a place in a protection centre, spend the next year learning Spanish and, once he turns 18, find work as a barber. What he fears most is ending up without legal documentation and seeing that plan collapse before it has even begun.

Leaving is not on his agenda, however. “All I need,” he said, “is a chance.”

world.title: Anti-LGBTQ+ laws are on the rise across west Africa, campaigners warn
world.snippet: Activists in the region say politicians regard LGBTQ+ people as ‘the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power’ A growing number of west...
world.content:
A growing number of west African countries are implementing or strengthening anti-LGBTQ+ laws, amid local political pressures and a global pushback against LGBTQ+ rights.

In March, Senegal doubled the maximum prison sentence for gay sex to 10 years and criminalised the “promotion” of homosexuality. Niger criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February, the first time same-sex intimacy had been outlawed in the country.

Mali and Burkina Faso, which neighbours Niger, also criminalised same-sex relations for the first time in the last two years. All three are ruled by military juntas.

In June, Ghana, which already outlaws gay sex, passed a law criminalising LGBTQ+ “activities”. The bill, which hasn’t been signed into law by the president, is the latest iteration of a bill that was first introduced in 2021.

“What I see in all of them is a political opportunism,” said Anthony Oluoch of Pan Africa ILGA, a continental LGBT+ rights campaign group.

In some countries, he said, the new or harsher laws had been backed by religious groups and campaigns for “family values”, while in Burkina Faso, whose population is predominantly Muslim, the law was framed as boosting its sovereignty in opposition to the west. “Underneath that all, there’s a lot of transnational reinforcement,” Oluoch added.

LGBTQ+ people “are the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power”, said an activist in Burkina Faso, who could not be named for her security.

The impact on the community, even before the law was implemented, has been devastating, activists said. Thirteen transgender women were detained without trial from June to November last year, a HIV worker said, with the women reporting they had been beaten by a military unit that imprisoned them. After the law was passed, there have been at least two sets of convictions.

Police are entrapping LGBTQ+ people on social media and demanding they denounce other community members, said the HIV worker, who fled the country in May after he was named by someone who had been arrested.

Despite military president Ibrahim Traoré’s anti-western rhetoric, Burkina Faso has also caught the eye of anti-LGBTQ+ campaigners that include conservative, western Christian groups.

The African Inter-Parliamentary Conference on Family Values and Sovereignty, a forum that many argue has influenced anti-LGBTQ+ laws on the continent, will be held in Burkina Faso and then Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) next year, it was announced this year.

The first three conferences were held annually in Uganda, in east Africa, beginning in 2023. Uganda imposed the death penalty for some same-sex sexual acts that year.

According to US-based international reproductive rights organisation Ipas, the annual gatherings are supported by Family Watch International (FWI), an Arizona-based Christian campaign group that opposes abortion and comprehensive sex education (CSE). Also in attendance has been Dutch-founded lobby group Christian Council International, which promotes similar views.

At this year’s conference, hosted by Ghana’s parliament in June, the draft African Charter on Family Sovereignty and Values treaty was drawn up. It condemns abortion and CSE, states that gender is either male or female, and asserts that parental rights supersede children’s. A draft copy was published on FWI’s website.

The anti-LGBTQ+ bill passed by Ghana’s parliament is a “very effective political tool”, supported by powerful religious organisations in the country, said Amanda Odoi, a researcher at the University of Cape Coast.

Nonetheless, Odoi added: “These international actors were very key in empowering, supporting, funding, financing and giving voice to the anti-LGBT campaign.”

She noted the Ghana bill’s similarity to Uganda’s law, as well as its “alphabet soup” – the bill uses the acronym “LGBTTQAP+” – that includes words like “questioning” not commonly used in Ghana.

Bringing this year’s African parliamentary conference to Ghana was a deliberate decision due to the country’s influence on the continent, said Ebenezer Peegah, executive director of Rightify Ghana, an NGO that supports LGBTQ+ people.

“Ghana has a lot of credentials that Uganda does not have … some clout that other countries in Africa do not have,” said Peegah, listing Ghana’s stable democracy, free and fair elections and relative press freedom.

Across west Africa, LGBTQ+ people are suffering the consequences of the new and harsher laws. In Senegal, the law is also hindering HIV prevention for men who have sex with men and transgender women, who have higher rates of HIV prevalence, as well as lawyers representing LGBTQ+ people, said Marame Kane, a French-Senegalese activist based in Paris.

About 100 Senegalese people fled to the Gambia this year, although most had to return to Senegal as they had no money, according to a Gambian HIV worker.

Same-sex relations are already punishable with up to life in prison in the Gambia, while transgender women are criminalised by a cross-dressing ban. However, the HIV worker worried that the government could strengthen the laws, making HIV services even harder to provide.

The crackdown in Senegal had also increased homophobia in the Gambia, he said, adding, “Gambia and Senegal share the same culture, the same religion, literally everything.”
